Intro to Machine Learning; Linear Regression Models

import pandas as pd

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression

Music Challenge

Which popular songs from the past will be recognized by future generations, and which will fade into obscurity? The website The Pudding conducts the Music Challenge where they ask thousands of people whether they recognize hit songs from the past. We’ll look at some of the data related to the article “Defining the 90s Music Canon”.

The data set at https://raw.githubusercontent.com/the-pudding/song-decay-clean/refs/heads/master/src/assets/data/lollipop_chart_data_july_13.csv contains 344 songs released in the 1990s. For each song, the proportion of survey respondents who recognized the song is recorded, for both Millennial respondents and Gen Z respondents. Our goal will be to use linear regression to predict the Gen Z recognition.

We will try several different linear regression models. Save each of your models with a different name because you will compare them at the end.

  1. Read in the data and describe the Gen Z recognition variable.
df_songs = pd.read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/the-pudding/song-decay-clean/refs/heads/master/src/assets/data/lollipop_chart_data_july_13.csv")
print(df_songs.shape)
display(df_songs.head())

print(df_songs["mean_gen_z_recognition"].describe())

df_songs["mean_gen_z_recognition"].plot.hist(bins=30, edgecolor="black")

plt.title("Distribution of Gen Z recognition")
plt.show()

  1. Use scikit-learn to fit a linear regression model for predicting Gen Z recognition from Millennial recognition.
X = df_songs[["mean_millennial_recognition"]]
y = df_songs["mean_gen_z_recognition"]

linear_model = LinearRegression()
linear_model.fit(X, y)

linear_model.coef_, linear_model.intercept_
(array([0.70673118]), np.float64(-0.04814972198183051))
  1. Make a scatterplot of Gen Z recognition versus Millennial recognition, and overlay a graph of the fitted model from the previous part.
x_grid = pd.DataFrame({"mean_millennial_recognition": np.linspace(0, 1, 200)})

plt.scatter(df_songs["mean_millennial_recognition"], df_songs["mean_gen_z_recognition"], alpha=0.5)
plt.plot(x_grid["mean_millennial_recognition"], linear_model.predict(x_grid), color="red", label="Linear model")
plt.xlabel("Millennial recognition")
plt.ylabel("Gen Z recognition")
plt.legend()
plt.show()
  1. Explain why you might want to consider taking a log of Gen Z recognition. Then use scikit-learn to fit a linear regression model for predicting log of Gen Z recognition from Millennial recognition.
# Gen Z recognition is right-skewed and the relationship with Millennial recognition is curved
# (Gen Z recognition stays low until Millennial recognition gets high, then rises quickly).
# A log transformation reduces the skew, makes the relationship closer to linear, and
# guarantees predictions on the original scale are positive.
y_log = np.log(df_songs["mean_gen_z_recognition"])

log_model = LinearRegression()
log_model.fit(X, y_log)

log_model.coef_, log_model.intercept_
(array([2.79916804]), np.float64(-2.9082912239452847))
  1. Make a scatterplot of Gen Z recognition versus Millennial recognition, and overlay a graph of the fitted model from the previous part.
plt.scatter(df_songs["mean_millennial_recognition"], df_songs["mean_gen_z_recognition"], alpha=0.5)
# model predicts log(Gen Z), so exponentiate to get back to the original scale
plt.plot(x_grid["mean_millennial_recognition"], np.exp(log_model.predict(x_grid)), color="red", label="Log model")
plt.xlabel("Millennial recognition")
plt.ylabel("Gen Z recognition")
plt.legend()
plt.show()
  1. Now we’ll try a polynomial model for predicting Gen Z recognition from Millennial recognition. Use scikit-learn to fit a model with two features: Millennial recognition and its square.
df_songs["mean_millennial_recognition_sq"] = df_songs["mean_millennial_recognition"] ** 2
X_sq = df_songs[["mean_millennial_recognition", "mean_millennial_recognition_sq"]]

square_model = LinearRegression()
square_model.fit(X_sq, y)

  1. Choose one of your favorite songs that is in the data set. Use each model to predict the Gen Z recognition for the song. Which model gives the best prediction?
def predict_all(millennial):
    x1 = pd.DataFrame({"mean_millennial_recognition": [millennial]})
    x2 = x1.assign(mean_millennial_recognition_sq=millennial ** 2)
    return pd.Series({
        "linear": linear_model.predict(x1)[0],
        "log": np.exp(log_model.predict(x1)[0]),
        "quadratic": square_model.predict(x2)[0],
    })

song = df_songs[df_songs["artist_song"] == "Backstreet Boys, The|||Everybody"]
display(song)

preds = predict_all(song["mean_millennial_recognition"].iloc[0])
actual = song["mean_gen_z_recognition"].iloc[0]
print(preds)
print("Actual Gen Z recognition:", actual)
print("Absolute errors:")
print((preds - actual).abs())

# Actual Gen Z recognition is ~0.857. The log model (~0.817) is closest, then the quadratic
# model (~0.799); the linear model (~0.635) badly underpredicts this very well-known song.

Categorical Predictors (FEV data)

Do non-smokers have better lungs than smokers? One measure of lung function is forced expiratory volume (FEV), the amount of air (in liters) an individual can exhale in the first second of forceful breath. Larger values of FEV are indicative of better functioning lungs. In a study, FEV was measured for a group of 654 subjects, along with whether or not they smoked and other variables.

df_fev = pd.read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/kevindavisross/data301/refs/heads/main/data/FEV.csv")

1. First fit a regression model with a single predictor: Smoking status. Since this variable is categorical you need to “dummify” it before fitting the model.

df_fev_dummies = pd.get_dummies(df_fev, columns=["Smoking status"], drop_first=True, dtype=int)
display(df_fev_dummies.head())

X_smoke = df_fev_dummies[["Smoking status_smoker"]]
y_fev = df_fev_dummies["FEV"]

smoke_model = LinearRegression()
smoke_model.fit(X_smoke, y_fev)

smoke_model.coef_, smoke_model.intercept_

2. What are the predictions from this model? How could we have known that those would be the predictions?

X_pred = pd.DataFrame({"Smoking status_smoker": [0, 1]})
print("Predictions (non-smoker, smoker):", smoke_model.predict(X_pred))

# With a single categorical predictor, the predictions are just the group means of FEV:
df_fev.groupby("Smoking status")["FEV"].mean()
Predictions (non-smoker, smoker): [2.56614261 3.27686154]
Smoking status
non-smoker    2.566143
smoker        3.276862
Name: FEV, dtype: float64

3. Look at the results for the previous parts. What do you notice? Is this what you expected? Remember: larger FEV means better lungs - who tends to have larger FEV, smokers or non-smokers?

The intercept is the mean FEV for non-smokers and the coefficient is positive, so smokers have a higher predicted (mean) FEV than non-smokers. This is surprising - we would expect smoking to hurt lung function, so smokers should have lower FEV.

4. Suggest some explanations for why smokers tend to have higher FEV than non-smokers?

  • Age is a confounder: the subjects are children/teens. Smokers in the study tend to be older, and older kids are bigger with larger lungs, so they have higher FEV regardless of smoking.
  • Similarly, smokers tend to be taller (height is related to age and lung capacity).
  • The study is observational, so the comparison of smokers and non-smokers isn’t controlling for these other differences.

5. Fit a linear regression model with two predictors: smoking status and Age (and no interaction).

X_add = df_fev_dummies[["Smoking status_smoker", "Age (months)"]]

additive_model = LinearRegression()
additive_model.fit(X_add, y_fev)

additive_model.coef_, additive_model.intercept_
(array([-0.21717836,  0.01921171]), np.float64(0.36814675002691644))

6. Make a scatterplot of FEV versus Age, colored by smoking status, and overlay a graph of the fitted model.

age_grid = np.linspace(df_fev["Age (months)"].min(), df_fev["Age (months)"].max(), 100)
colors = {0: "tab:blue", 1: "tab:orange"}
labels = {0: "non-smoker", 1: "smoker"}

for s in [0, 1]:
    sub = df_fev_dummies[df_fev_dummies["Smoking status_smoker"] == s]
    plt.scatter(sub["Age (months)"], sub["FEV"], alpha=0.4, color=colors[s], label=labels[s])
    grid = pd.DataFrame({"Smoking status_smoker": s, "Age (months)": age_grid})
    plt.plot(age_grid, additive_model.predict(grid), color=colors[s], linewidth=2)

plt.xlabel("Age (months)")
plt.ylabel("FEV (liters)")
plt.title("Additive model: smoking status + age")
plt.legend()
plt.show()

7. Fit a linear regression model with predictors smoking status, Age, and their interaction.

df_fev_dummies["smoker_x_age"] = df_fev_dummies["Smoking status_smoker"] * df_fev_dummies["Age (months)"]
X_int = df_fev_dummies[["Smoking status_smoker", "Age (months)", "smoker_x_age"]]

interaction_model = LinearRegression()
interaction_model.fit(X_int, y_fev)

interaction_model.coef_, interaction_model.intercept_
(array([ 1.8700573 ,  0.02016168, -0.01311012]),
 np.float64(0.25946202327124324))

8. Make a scatterplot of FEV versus Age, colored by smoking status, and overlay a graph of the fitted model.

for s in [0, 1]:
    sub = df_fev_dummies[df_fev_dummies["Smoking status_smoker"] == s]
    plt.scatter(sub["Age (months)"], sub["FEV"], alpha=0.4, color=colors[s], label=labels[s])
    grid = pd.DataFrame({"Smoking status_smoker": s, "Age (months)": age_grid})
    grid["smoker_x_age"] = grid["Smoking status_smoker"] * grid["Age (months)"]
    plt.plot(age_grid, interaction_model.predict(grid), color=colors[s], linewidth=2)

plt.xlabel("Age (months)")
plt.ylabel("FEV (liters)")
plt.title("Interaction model: smoking status * age")
plt.legend()
plt.show()

9. Compare the models. Which do you think is “best”? Why? How could you investigate?

  • The smoking-only model is misleading because it ignores age (a confounder): smokers have about 0.71 L higher FEV on average. Once age is included (additive model), the smoking coefficient flips to about -0.22 L: at the same age, smokers have lower FEV.
  • The interaction model lets the age slope differ by smoking status: FEV rises about 0.020 L/month for non-smokers but only about 0.020 - 0.013 = 0.007 L/month for smokers, consistent with smoking slowing lung growth. It is the most flexible and seems to fit the plot best.
  • To investigate which is “best”, we could compare the models on how well they predict new data - e.g., split into training/test sets (or use cross-validation) and compare test error (MSE/RMSE) or \(R^2\). We’d also check residual plots for patterns.
